analysis.one_liner: Bans payday lending above 36% interest unless a state licenses and tightly regulates payday lenders.
analysis.headline: The bill never came to a vote: it sat in a House Banking subcommittee from May 1999 until the Congress ended in January 2001, despite 24 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make payday loans — short-term loans backed by a post-dated check or electronic debit — illegal in any state unless that state licenses payday lenders and imposes federal minimum rules. Those rules include a 36% annual interest cap, a $300 maximum loan, a $5 maximum administrative fee, no rollovers, a ban on using criminal charges to collect, and private lawsuits for violations. It would also bar banks from making payday loans above 36% interest or financing payday lenders who break state law.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income borrowers who use payday loans, most often workers who run short before payday. They would get a hard 36% interest ceiling, a $300 loan cap, a $5 fee cap, minimum loan terms, a ban on rollovers that trap people in repeated debt, and a ban on lenders threatening criminal action over a bounced check. Borrowers could also sue for damages, and lenders would owe at least $1,000 per day of violation.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the annual percentage rate on any payday loan at 36%, or the state's own lower cap, whichever is smaller.

Caps loan principal at $300 and administrative fees at $5, requires a minimum loan term of two weeks for each $50 borrowed, and bans refinancing or rolling over a loan past its due date — the mechanism that repeatedly extends payday debt.

Prohibits lenders from initiating or threatening criminal complaints when a borrower's check or electronic transfer fails, and requires posted and written disclosures of loan terms and borrower rights.

Requires states to license payday lenders, review the character and finances of owners, hold public hearings, keep complaint records public, and impose civil and criminal penalties, including at least $1,000 per day for violations and private rights of action for borrowers.

Bars banks and other insured institutions from making payday loans above 36% APR or from lending money to payday lenders who are not in full compliance with state law — cutting off a common channel banks used to run payday lending.

analysis.who_pays: Payday lenders lose their core business model, which typically charges far more than 36% on two-week loans. Banks financing payday lenders lose that revenue stream. Credit insurers lose premiums on policies sold with payday loans. Borrowers who cannot qualify for bank credit could lose access to any legal short-term loan in states where a 36% rate is unprofitable.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders and their bank financiers

drawbacks.text: A 36% APR cap makes traditional two-week, small-dollar loans unprofitable, so in states that do not adopt the federal framework the product disappears rather than gets cheaper — borrowers who relied on it could be pushed to unlicensed or illegal lenders.

The bill sets loan terms from Washington: a $300 principal cap, a $5 fee cap, and a minimum term of two weeks per $50 borrowed, overriding states that had chosen to permit higher-cost, larger, or faster products.
Legality would hinge on the Federal Reserve Board's determination that a state's law meets every listed requirement, adding a federal gatekeeper over state consumer-credit choices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers, the protections are substantial: a 36% ceiling, an end to rollover debt, and real penalties and lawsuits would eliminate the most expensive features of payday lending. The honest tradeoff is access — the same cap that protects borrowers also makes the product unviable, and people who used it would need somewhere else to turn. The bill acknowledged this by allowing states to keep the product only if they adopted the full licensing and price framework, but it offered no replacement source of small-dollar credit.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its Financial Institutions subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Rush introduced the Payday Borrower Protection Act of 1999 on May 5, 1999.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Banking and Financial Services.
On May 28, 1999, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit.
No further action was taken — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

The bill would have prohibited payday loans in any state unless that state licensed and regulated lenders under a framework including a 36% APR cap, a $300 loan limit, a $5 fee cap, a rollover ban, and a ban on criminal collection threats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Payday lenders, and the banks that financed them, kept operating under the rules of the late 1990s for the remainder of the Congress, with no federal interest cap or licensing mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Payday lenders and their bank financiers

for.name: Rep. Bobby L. Rush
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 5, 1999 and delivered introductory remarks.

for.name: 24 of 211 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on May 28, 1999 and took no further action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 28, 1999 and never reported it out or scheduled a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 25 named supporters — the sponsor and 24 cosponsors — were House Democrats, and the bill died without action in a committee system run by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill outlaws the standard payday loan model in any state that does not adopt the federal framework: a 36% APR cap, $300 maximum, $5 fee cap, and no rollovers would end the high-cost short-term product the industry sells. Its revenue comes from fees that would be illegal under the bill.

The bill bars insured banks from making payday loans above 36% APR or lending to payday lenders who do not comply with state law, cutting off the partnership channel by which banks carried payday lending.
The bill bans any additional fee or premium for credit insurance sold alongside a payday loan, eliminating premiums on policies sold to payday borrowers.
